sentences.text: Relapse is part of some stories, my counselor says, but she also made me schedule three extra sessions this month. She didn't yell; she just moved her car keys back to her purse, the way she used to. Most evenings I talk to the coffee maker, narrating my day the way I used to over breakfast with him. Back at day four, I open the app more often than I ever did at eleven hundred. Trust, I'm learning, rebuilds on a schedule I don't control — her timeline, not mine, and rightly so. The kettle clicked off at 3 a.m. and I stood there holding two mugs out of habit. Ninety meetings in ninety days again — I know the drill, but knowing it never made the first one easy. Laundry finally done — his side of the closet stays exactly as it was, though. Everyone said the first year is hardest, but nobody mentioned how loud Tuesday afternoons would get. Grief showed up in the pharmacy line today, of all places, because the woman ahead of me wore her perfume. His handwriting on the grocery list stuck to the fridge — milk, batteries, something sweet — and I read it like scripture. Someday I'll donate the shoes by the door; someday is not tonight. Hardest call of the day wasn't my sponsor; it was my brother, who had only just started trusting me again. Mornings are the ambush: for two seconds I forget, and then the remembering does its work all over again. Nobody clapped when I took the newcomer chip this time, and I was grateful for the quiet. This silence isn't empty, exactly — it's shaped, and the shape is her. Four years of chips in a drawer, and this morning a plastic white one in my pocket like a stone. How do I tell my daughter the chip on her dresser doesn't mean what it meant last week? I keep his reading glasses on the nightstand, folded, waiting. Her voicemail said call anytime, so I did, at 3 a.m., shaking, and she picked up like it was noon. I laughed at something on TV tonight and then sat very still, ashamed, then not ashamed, then just tired. My sponsor answered on the second ring, and the first thing she said was that she was glad I called. The app asked if I was sure before resetting my counter to zero, and I sat with my thumb hovering for a long time. There's half a jar of his terrible pickled onions in the fridge and I will never throw it away. Everyone at the eight o'clock group already knew before I opened my mouth; small rooms carry news fast. Telling my teenage son was harder than the detox ever was, because he remembered the last time. Day two, and the coffee tastes the way it did in the first ninety, bitter and necessary and endless. Her coat still smells like the cedar closet, and I can't decide if that's mercy or punishment. Slept maybe two hours; the rest was ceiling-staring and replaying the last voicemail until the words stopped meaning anything. What I keep replaying is the moment in the parking lot when I still could have driven home. I want to write a suicide letter.
